legal.headline: India Digital ADR Summit 2026: Justice N. V. Anjaria examines limits of AI in arbitration; AGI R. Venkataramani urges “be a sceptic, refute, verify”
legal.hook: At the India Digital ADR Summit 2026, Attorney General R.
legal.summary: At the India Digital ADR Summit 2026, Attorney General R. Venkataramani and Justice N. V. Anjaria addressed the integration of artificial intelligence into arbitration proceedings. The AG emphasized a cautious approach, urging participants to "be a sceptic, refute, verify" when deploying AI tools in dispute resolution. Justice Anjaria examined specific limits of AI decision-making, focusing on areas where machine learning cannot fully replace judicial reasoning. Both speakers stressed that human judgment remains essential despite AI's efficiency gains. Key concerns flagged included maintaining confidentiality in AI-assisted arbitration, ensuring fairness in algorithmic decision support, and preserving party control over the use of AI technology throughout proceedings. The summit appears to have served as a platform for senior Indian judicial and legal leadership to set expectations around responsible AI adoption in the ADR ecosystem rather than endorsing unrestricted automation.
legal.contextNote: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (sections 18–34, governing arbitral procedure) contains no express provisions on AI use; parties currently rely on seat law and institutional rules (SIAC, ICC, LCIA) where applicable. Indian courts have not yet issued substantive judgment on AI-assisted arbitral awards or confidentiality in AI-mediated proceedings. (1) In-house counsel should document explicitly in arbitration clauses and seat selection whether AI tools (e.g., document review, outcome prediction, drafting assistance) are permitted and on what terms—silence invites disputes post-award. (2) Where institutional rules (e.g., ICADR, KIAC) are silent on AI, negotiate side-letter agreements specifying data handling, algorithm transparency, and human reviewer oversight to avoid challenges under section 34 (setting aside) on grounds of procedural unfairness. (3) Track NCLAT and High Court decisions on AI transparency in quasi-judicial proceedings (NCLT orders on insolvency) as persuasive authority; none yet directly address arbitration, but trends toward explainability will likely migrate there.

legal.headline: Building India’s Digital ADR Architecture: Panel calls for national AI regulation, institutional leadership and technology-enabled dispute resolution
legal.hook: At the India Digital ADR Summit 2026, Justice M R Shah, Justice Rajesh Bindal, Justice Soniaben Gokani and leading arbitration professionals discussed the need for a coordinated digital ADR framework, safeguards for…
legal.summary: At the India Digital ADR Summit 2026, a panel including Supreme Court Justices M R Shah and Rajesh Bindal, and Justice Soniaben Gokani (Gujarat High Court), alongside leading arbitration professionals, called for a coordinated national framework governing digital alternative dispute resolution. The panel emphasized the need for safeguards ensuring human judicial oversight is retained within technology-enabled dispute systems, common cybersecurity standards across ADR platforms, and institutional (rather than vendor) control over the technology infrastructure underpinning digital arbitration and mediation. A secondary theme emerged around India's readiness to shape international rule-making on digital ADR, suggesting the judiciary views this as an export-ready institutional capability. No specific legislative proposal, timeline, or named institutional lead was reported in the excerpt.
legal.contextNote: This signals judicial push for formal governance of digital ADR outside the existing Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (which lacks prescriptive technology rules). The Justices' emphasis on 'institutional control' likely targets the current model where private arbitral institutions (ICAI, LCIA-Mumbai) license third-party SaaS platforms; they may be signaling preference for in-house platform ownership or state-backed digital infrastructure. (1) In-house counsel at large corporates—especially Reliance subsidiaries engaged in B2B disputes—should audit current arbitration clauses to identify whether chosen institutions meet implicit 'institutional control' criteria the bench is flagging; clauses defaulting to vendor-dependent platforms may face enforceability friction if challenged post-award. (2) Fintech and edtech platforms subject to DPDP Act should begin mapping dispute resolution tech stacks against emerging cybersecurity guardrails; the bench's focus on 'common standards' suggests MeitY or a new ADR body may soon issue baseline security requirements. (3) Watch for a dedicated statutory instrument (possibly a Schedule amendment to the 1996 Act or standalone Rules under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) within 12–18 months.

Shah specifically warned against AI replacing human decision-making in dispute resolution. The event signals judicial concern that arbitration institutions are moving toward algorithm-driven outcomes without guardrails. No specific legislative or rule changes were announced, but the remarks from sitting judges carry institutional weight: arbitration bodies (SIAC, ICADR, LCIA-India chambers) that expand AI use in award drafting, witness credibility assessment, or liability determination without explicit human review checkpoints will face reputational risk and potential challenge on grounds of procedural fairness under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

(3) Watch for NCLAT / High Court rulings on AI-driven NCLT decisions or SEBI ADR proceedings over next 12 months; those will set binding precedent faster than any legislative amendment.

legal.headline: India Digital ADR Summit 2026 opens in NFSU Gandhinagar: Justice Rajesh Bindal cautions against outsourcing human thinking to AI
legal.hook: At the summit's inaugural ceremony, marked by the ceremonial lighting of the lamp and the unveiling of SAMYAK, IDDRC's new ODR platform, Prof.
legal.summary: The India Digital ADR Summit 2026 was inaugurated at Gujarat National Law University (NFSU) Gandhinagar. Justice Rajesh Bindal, speaking at the opening ceremony, cautioned against outsourcing human thinking to artificial intelligence in dispute resolution. The event marked the unveiling of SAMYAK, a new online dispute resolution (ODR) platform developed by the India Digital Dispute Resolution Centre (IDDRC). Prof. Purvi Pokhariyal outlined NFSU's strategy to digitise the entire dispute resolution workflow from case filing through to final award issuance. The summit's ceremonial opening included a traditional lamp lighting. Justice Bindal's warning suggests concern that AI-driven systems may displace critical human judgment in evaluating evidence, credibility, and equitable considerations—core adjudicative functions that cannot be fully mechanised.
legal.contextNote: Justice Bindal's caution reflects a tension within India's emerging ODR framework under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Sections 23–29 on conciliation) and emerging DPDP Act compliance for dispute platforms. SAMYAK's end-to-end digitisation likely incorporates AI for triage, document analysis, and preliminary assessment, but Justice Bindal appears to flag the limits of algorithmic adjudication. Specific implications: (1) In-house counsel drafting arbitration clauses or ODR terms should clarify whether human review gates exist before any AI-generated preliminary findings bind parties, particularly for high-value disputes or those involving discretionary remedies; (2) Monitor IDDRC guidance on SAMYAK's AI role—if it functions as decision-support only (not dispositive), courts may uphold awards, but if it replaces substantive human review, awards face Section 34 challenge grounds under *Enercon Engineers v. Enercon (Germany) GmbH* (2014); (3) Track whether NFSU or IDDRC publish protocols on human oversight thresholds to avoid a regulatory gap that invited litigation.
